blocks.title: Out to the island — the early ferry

transit.label: JR Sanyō line — Hiroshima → Miyajimaguchi
transit.detail: About twenty-three minutes. Go early: the shrine opens at 06:30, and the mountain has to be behind you in daylight.
transit.cost_note: one way — the round trip on this line is ¥840

transit.label: JR ferry — Miyajimaguchi → Miyajima
transit.detail: Ten minutes, about four sailings an hour. The 9:10–16:10 crossings loop past the great torii when the tide allows.
transit.payment: No ticket to buy. Tap once at the gate inside the Miyajimaguchi terminal before you walk down to the boat — that one tap takes the ¥200 fare and the ¥100 island tax together. On the boat itself there is nothing to do.
transit.cost_note: ¥200 of fare plus the ¥100 Miyajima visitor tax, which is collected on the outbound leg only and bundled into a single ¥300 ticket; an IC tap at the gate pays both at once

items.detail: Twelve to fifteen minutes along the foreshore from the pier, then forty to forty-five minutes inside. A one-way circuit of corridors standing on pillars over the water, the Marōdo shrine, the hirabutai platform and the Noh stage of 1680, built out over the sea — so the resonating jar that normally sits under a Noh floor cannot, and the floor itself is made to carry the sound of the feet. The combined ticket adds the Treasure Hall — take it only if you want it; the day does not need it. The East Corridor — the entry leg of the one-way circuit — is under structural reinforcement until December 2026, which covers this date. The shrine has announced no closure or diversion, and its construction page is where one would appear.

Eight minutes up from the shrine, about twenty-five minutes there. Hideyoshi’s 1587 sutra hall, 857 tatami, left with no ceiling and no front wall because he died before it was finished — you walk into an unfinished building. The five-storey pagoda beside it is fully wrapped for repair and cannot be seen as itself; the scaffolding stands until 20 November 2027, so it outlasts this trip by a year. It closes at 16:30, an hour before Itsukushima Shrine.

Fifteen minutes on the lanes from Senjōkaku, then forty-five minutes to an hour. The Shingon head temple of the Omuro school: the henjōkutsu cave lined with the eighty-eight icons of the Shikoku pilgrimage, sutra wheels set into the stair handrail, ranks of rakan. It is free, it is the last thing before the climb, and the Misen trailhead starts here.

maps.label: Misen trail map — Miyajima Tourist Association
maps.note: All three official routes up Misen, including the Daishō-in course we climb and the Momijidani course we come down.

maps.label: AllTrails — Daishō-in course
maps.note: The ascent we are doing: stone staircase most of the way, through the Jizō statues.

transit.label: On foot — Daishō-in → the summit of Misen
transit.detail: 2.6 km and 535 m from sea level, stone steps almost the whole way, marked by the twenty-four chō stones and entering the inscribed primeval forest from the bottom. The tourism association gives an hour and a half to two hours including rests; sources pricing the whole mountain on foot say three to five hours; plan on two to two and a half hours up. It is rated harder than the Momijidani course and is steeper underfoot than Takao — the hardest single effort of the trip. Nothing is sold on the mountain: carry food and water.

items.detail: Forty-five minutes to an hour on the plateau: Misen Hondō, the Kuguri-iwa rock arch, and the 535 m observation deck over the Setouchi archipelago. The deck is open 10:00–16:00 and the day clears that with hours in hand. Reikadō burnt out in May 2026 and has no rebuild timeline — assume it is gone; the flame itself survived and is kept sub-divided.

transit.label: On foot — down to Momijidani and the town
transit.detail: The gentler of the two courses, an hour and a quarter to an hour and a half down — faster than the ascent but not half of it, because it is stone step and root the whole way. It lands at Momijidani Park, fifteen minutes from the Omotesandō street where the late lunch sits: anago-meshi, grilled Setouchi oysters, momiji-manjū off the griddle. The pier is the far end of that same street. If the climb has run long, come down the way you went up: the temple's own advice is that the Daishō-in course stays light longer, and Momijidani is a valley that darkens early. If your legs are finished at the top, the ropeway is the alternative descent — but take it by about 14:30 or not at all: November is its busiest month, the descent queue is the notorious one and can run to an hour on a Sunday, the last car down is 16:30, and the only fallback to a queue is this walk, which you do not want to begin at dusk.

blocks.title: The old lanes and the foreshore at dusk

items.label: Machiya-dōri, then the torii as the light goes
items.detail: About forty-five minutes, and the one thing on the day that closes at no hour — the summit deck shuts at 16:00, Senjōkaku at 16:30, Daishō-in at 17:00 and the shrine at 17:30 — so it takes up whatever ran late. The back lane behind the tourist street, then the shore. Sunset is 17:12 and civil dusk 17:38, and you are down off the mountain around 14:45, so this is an unhurried end to the day.

transit.label: JR ferry — Miyajima 17:25 → Miyajimaguchi
transit.detail: Ten minutes. This leg is nowhere near a last service: 17:40, 17:55, 18:10, 18:25 and 18:40 follow, then 19:00, 19:30, 20:00, 20:42, 21:25 and 22:14 last — and a second operator runs the same crossing on its own hulls.
transit.payment: Tap at the gate on the Miyajima pier before boarding, the same as this morning — ¥200 this time, with no island tax on the way back — that is collected only on the crossing over.
transit.cost_note: the return leg is fare only — the ¥100 visitor tax was paid outbound

transit.label: JR Sanyō line — Miyajimaguchi 17:49 → Hiroshima 18:20
transit.detail: Thirty-one minutes, not the twenty-three of the morning: this is an all-stations train, and the twenty-two-minute run belongs to a rapid service you cannot be on. Three more follow at 18:03, 18:19 and 18:31, then trains every fifteen to twenty minutes until the last at 23:27, and the Hiroden tram from Hiroden-Miyajimaguchi is a third, fully independent way into the city. Dinner tonight wants a last order no earlier than 20:30 — this is the evening of the hardest day of the trip, on a return leg that is a ladder.
transit.cost_note: one way — the round trip on this line is ¥840

notes_top: 💴 Cash on the island: the shrine gate, the lunch counters on the Omotesandō street, and the ropeway's ¥2,000 return if you use it. The ferry is the exception — one tap at the gate covers it, with no counter and no errand.

backup.title: If it rains — the island keeps its halls and loses its mountain
backup.detail: A washout keeps Itsukushima Shrine, Senjōkaku, Daishō-in and the Treasure Hall, and adds the Miyajima Public Aquarium — ¥1,420, 9:00 to 17:00, last admission 16:00 — for about five hours in all, a half-day. The Miyajima History and Folklore Museum is a second indoor option and is available only because this is a Sunday: it closes on Mondays. This is a large loss: what goes is the climb up through the inscribed primeval forest and the summit, which is the reason the day exists.

blocks.title: Check out by 11:00 — the morning is free

items.detail: Breakfast, then out of the room by 11:00. The 2nd-floor self-cloak covers the check-out day as well, so the bags go back in there and the last hour and a half is genuinely free — the same IC-card lock as on arrival, with the station coin lockers as the fallback. Nothing is planned for this morning — spend it however you like.

transit.label: Walk — the hotel to Hiroshima Station
transit.detail: Three hundred metres, four minutes.

blocks.title: Ekiben — bought before the Shinkansen gates

items.detail: There is about ninety minutes of slack here, so this is unhurried — the opposite of the Tokyo ekiben stop. The shop is on ekie’s 2nd floor, outside the ticket gates, on the concourse between the hotel side of the station and the Shinkansen gates: buy first, then go through, because once you are inside it is behind you. The box to look for is Ueno’s anago-meshi bentō, sold since 1901 and named for the island you spent yesterday on; it is delivered in and can sell out. If it has, six counters inside the Shinkansen gates trade on a Monday, one of them on your own platform — but Musashi’s in-gate bentō kitchen, the best-known name in this station, is the one that shuts on Mondays.

transit.label: Nozomi 26 — Hiroshima 12:43 → Tokyo 16:33
transit.detail: Three hours fifty. Seat E is the Fuji side going east, visible around 15:35–15:55. If you miss it, six more follow — 13:07, 13:22, 13:29, 13:43, 14:03 and 14:18 — and the midday train still leaves about five hours of margin against a hotel desk that closes at 22:00.
transit.cost_note: flexible smartEX, reserved — every train in the ladder can be taken at no extra cost; the same seat at a station counter is ¥19,760

transit.label: JR — Tokyo → Akihabara
transit.detail: Two stops on the Yamanote or the Keihin-Tōhoku, about four minutes. With bags, reckon twenty to twenty-five minutes from the Shinkansen platform to the hotel door.
transit.cost_note: IC fare, tapping Suica; the paper ticket is ¥160.

transit.label: Walk — Akihabara Station to the hotel

items.detail: The same property as the first stay, booked separately. The desk takes check-ins from 14:00 to 22:00 and that close is hard; arriving about 16:55 leaves roughly five hours of margin. The booking cannot be date-changed. ¥48,360 for the two nights plus about ¥400 of Tokyo lodging tax is paid at the property — nothing was prepaid. Nothing follows dinner tonight.

transit.label: JR Chūō-Sōbu — Akihabara → Koishikawa-Kōrakuen
transit.detail: Chūō-Sōbu line to Iidabashi, then the walk to the garden gate. The gates open at 09:00, an hour and a half before the museum does, which is why the garden is the morning.
transit.cost_note: the day’s whole JR fare — Akihabara to Iidabashi (¥155) and on east to Ryōgoku (¥199). It is priced as one figure and is not split between the two rides, so it sits here on the first of them. IC fares, tapping Suica.

items.detail: An hour to an hour and a half. Tokyo’s oldest surviving Edo daimyō garden, begun in 1629 by the Mito Tokugawa, and the rare place that is both a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and a Special Historic Site. Its landscape sets Japanese and Chinese scenes side by side — the Engetsu-kyō full-moon bridge, the Tsūten-kyō, a miniature Ōi-gawa and a rice field. Last entry is 16:30, but the morning is where this belongs.

transit.label: JR Chūō-Sōbu — Iidabashi → Ryōgoku
transit.detail: Back to Iidabashi and on east, about fifteen minutes. The fare is already counted on the way out. Lunch is chanko-nabe in the sumo district — the wrestlers’ stew is Ryōgoku’s own dish — and the museum is a few minutes from the station.

items.detail: Two and a half to three hours, and it takes them. Reopened on 31 March 2026 after a four-year renewal into an immersive museum: a walk-in Nakamura-za playhouse, a tenement room you can now enter, the 26-metre Nihonbashi span and the full-scale Hattori clock tower of 1890s Ginza, and projection-mapped galleries running Edo into Tokyo. Last admission is half an hour before the close; no booking is needed and same-day tickets are sold at the door.

transit.label: Toei Ōedo — Ryōgoku → Kiyosumi-teien
transit.detail: Two stops to Kiyosumi-shirakawa, then the walk. Get there before 16:30, which is the garden’s last entry.
transit.cost_note: an estimate, and it covers the ride home as well as this one — it assumes you take Kiyosumi. Skip it and the return is a different route at a different fare.

items.detail: Forty minutes to an hour, and the day works without it — this is how you make the day longer or shorter, decided on the day itself. A stroll garden built around the Daisensui pond, with famous named stones set along the circuit and the Ryōtei pavilion standing out over the water.

transit.label: Ōedo then JR Chūō-Sōbu — Kiyosumi-shirakawa → Akihabara, changing at Ryōgoku
transit.detail: The way you came, in reverse: the Ōedo two stops back to Ryōgoku, then the Chūō-Sōbu two stops to Akihabara. Twenty to thirty minutes with the walk out of the garden; the fare is counted on the leg out. Skip Kiyosumi and you are already standing at Ryōgoku — the Chūō-Sōbu goes straight home from there and that fare is not spent at all.

blocks.title: One errand for today — the Skyliner seat

items.label: Reserve the seat for tomorrow’s Skyliner
items.detail: The return half of the round-trip Skyliner ticket carries no seat, and tomorrow morning is not the time to discover that. Take the coupon and your passport to either the Keisei Ueno ticket counter or the Nippori JR-connection counter today, while you are in town all day, and have the 11:05 out of Nippori reserved.

backup.title: This day is the rain answer
backup.detail: Two and a half to three hours of it are indoors, inside the Edo-Tokyo Museum, and only the two gardens are exposed — both walkable in light rain. There is very little here for a wet forecast to take, which makes this the day to move a rained-out day into if either of the last two Tokyo days needs it. It has no weather fallback of its own because it does not need one.

items.detail: Check-out is 11:00 and breakfast is served early, but leave at about 10:30. That half hour costs you nothing and it is the only cushion you have between the tax-refund customs step and El Al's check-in close, which the ticket never states.

transit.label: JR — Akihabara → Nippori
transit.detail: Four stops, then ~7 min across to the Keisei platforms.
transit.cost_note: IC fare, tapping Suica; the paper ticket is ¥200.

transit.label: Skyliner — Nippori → Narita T1
transit.detail: 11:05 (No. 33), Terminal 1 at 11:44 — four hours and one minute before LY92. Miss it and 11:25 and 11:42 both still clear three hours; the ladder runs to 20:20. The seat for this leg is reserved at a counter on Nov 10, not on this morning.
transit.cost_note: the second of the two one-way Skyliner Discount e-tickets; walk-up is ¥2,570

items.detail: The ~10:30 leave lands you at T1 at 11:44, four hours and one minute before the flight. The target of being there by ~12:45 comes from the ~3 h security norm — El Al’s documented check-in close is blank on the ticket, so that norm is an assumption rather than a published time.

items.label: The tax refund step — only if you bought something on or after Nov 1
items.detail: Both shopping days sit on the old side of the switch, so the camera, the pen, the watch and the Uniqlo need nothing here. What can bite is incidental shopping from Nov 1 onward: that tax is refunded only after customs confirms the goods are leaving, and the confirmation happens before the El Al counter.
